figures.alt: Disposal of polymers, Edexcel IGCSE Chemistry

specPoints.text: explain problems in the disposal of addition polymers, including: their inertness and inability to biodegrade; the production of toxic gases when they are burned

primer.text: From Alkenes you already know how double bonds open up and join monomers into addition polymers with strong carbon-carbon backbones. This note follows those polymers to the end of their useful life, where their greatest strength becomes the planet's problem.

lessons.title: Why addition polymers resist breakdown
lessons.opening: The same strong carbon-carbon bonds that make addition polymers useful also make them nearly unreactive. Micro-organisms cannot break them down, so buried plastic simply sits there while landfill sites fill up. This lesson explains why inertness is an environmental liability.
keyPoints: Addition polymers are built from many small molecules joined by strong carbon-carbon bonds.
Those strong bonds make the polymers unreactive and chemically inert.
Inert polymers cannot biodegrade, so decomposers cannot break them down.
Landfill disposal takes up valuable land and sites fill up quickly.
The inability to biodegrade is the core disposal problem.

low.restatement: Strong carbon-carbon bonds make addition polymers unreactive and inert. Nothing in the soil can break them down, so landfill sites take up land and fill up fast.
low.analogy: An addition polymer in a landfill is like a stone in a field: the seasons pass, the microbes try, and the stone simply waits.
low.examPointer: Name the property first, inertness, then the consequence, inability to biodegrade; that chain of reasoning earns the marks.

medium.restatement: The strong carbon-carbon backbone makes addition polymers chemically inert, so micro-organisms such as decomposers cannot biodegrade them. Buried waste therefore occupies valuable land and fills sites quickly, which is why disposal is an environmental problem rather than a solved one.
medium.analogy: Their strength is a superpower with a bill: the same armour that survives every product lifetime also survives every refuse tip, indefinitely.
medium.examPointer: Quote both strands for landfill questions: inertness with non-biodegradability, and the space the buried waste consumes.

check.stem: Which bonds make addition polymers so unreactive?

options.text: Strong carbon-carbon bonds throughout the chain
options.explanation: The joining up of monomers leaves a backbone that ordinary chemistry struggles to attack.
Intermolecular forces decide melting, not chemical inertness of the chain itself.
The polymer chain is covalent; no ionic bonding holds it together.

options.text: Open double bonds left all along the chain
options.explanation: Addition polymerisation consumes the double bonds as the chain forms.

check.stem: What does it mean to describe an addition polymer as inert?

options.explanation: Inert means the substance resists chemical attack, which is why it persists.
Radioactivity has nothing to do with the disposal problem here.
Flammability is a separate hazard discussed under incineration.
Magnetism is irrelevant to polymer chemistry.

check.stem: Why can decomposers not break addition polymers down?

options.text: The polymers are non-biodegradable because their strong bonds resist attack
options.explanation: Inertness blocks the microbial chemistry that biodegradation depends on.

options.text: Decomposers simply refuse to eat plastic
options.explanation: Preference is not the mechanism; the bonds resist the chemistry.

options.text: Landfill sites are too cold for any life
options.explanation: Life thrives in landfill; the polymer itself is the obstacle.

options.text: The polymer molecules are too small to see
options.explanation: Visibility is irrelevant; molecules are always invisible.

check.stem: Which statement about landfill disposal of polymers is correct?

options.text: Sites fill up quickly because the buried polymer never breaks down
options.explanation: Permanent burial consumes space that natural decay would eventually free.

options.text: Polymers dissolve into the soil over time
options.explanation: Inert polymers neither dissolve nor decay in the soil.

options.text: Polymers evaporate from the site within years
options.explanation: Solid polymers do not evaporate at landfill temperatures.

options.text: Landfill naturally turns polymers into compost
options.explanation: Composting requires biodegradable material, which these polymers are not.

check.stem: Which phrase correctly describes the biodegradability of addition polymers?

options.explanation: The spec lists their inability to biodegrade as a named disposal problem.

options.text: They biodegrade within a few months
options.explanation: That describes natural materials, not addition polymers.

options.text: They biodegrade only in strong sunlight
options.explanation: Sunlight may weather surfaces but the spec does not grant biodegradation.

options.text: They biodegrade once buried and wet
options.explanation: Moisture does not unlock the strong carbon backbone.

lessons.title: Incineration and its three hazards
lessons.opening: Burning looks like a tidy answer, and incineration does release useful heat energy. But the smoke carries costs: carbon dioxide warms the climate, chlorine-bearing plastics release toxic hydrogen chloride, and incomplete burning makes poisonous carbon monoxide. This lesson weighs all three.
keyPoints: Burning polymers releases a lot of heat energy.
It also produces carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas linked to climate change.
Polymers containing chlorine, such as PVC, release toxic hydrogen chloride when burned.
Incomplete combustion during incineration produces carbon monoxide.
Carbon monoxide is toxic because it reduces the blood's capacity to carry oxygen.

low.restatement: Burning polymers gives out useful heat but produces carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. Chlorine-bearing plastics give toxic hydrogen chloride, and incomplete burning makes carbon monoxide, which harms the blood.
low.analogy: Incineration is a deal with strings: warmth today, then three separate letters of complaint from the climate, the chlorine and the blood.
low.examPointer: Keep the three hazards separate: dioxide for climate, hydrogen chloride for PVC, monoxide for incomplete burning.

medium.restatement: Incineration recovers a lot of heat energy but emits carbon dioxide, the greenhouse gas driving climate change. Polymers containing chlorine, such as PVC, release toxic hydrogen chloride gas, and any incomplete combustion adds carbon monoxide, which lowers the capacity of blood to carry oxygen.
medium.analogy: Think of the flue as a three-lane exit: one lane carries the climate bill, one carries chlorine's poison, and one carries the silent gas that crowds oxygen out of the blood.
medium.examPointer: Match each toxic gas to its trigger: hydrogen chloride needs chlorine in the polymer, monoxide needs incomplete combustion.

check.stem: Which greenhouse gas does burning polymers release?

options.explanation: The combustion of the carbon backbone releases it, contributing to climate change.
That gas is toxic rather than a greenhouse gas, and needs chlorine in the polymer.
Monoxide comes from incomplete burning and is toxic, not a greenhouse driver.
Methane is not listed among the combustion products here.

check.stem: Which polymer releases toxic hydrogen chloride when burned?

options.explanation: Chlorine in the chain leaves as hydrogen chloride gas on burning.

options.text: Polyethene, which contains only carbon and hydrogen
options.explanation: Without chlorine there is nothing to make hydrogen chloride.
Its hydroxyl groups do not supply chlorine either.
Polyesters carry oxygen but no chlorine, so no hydrogen chloride forms.

check.stem: Which gas forms when incineration is incomplete?

options.explanation: Limited oxygen supply leaves carbon only partly oxidised, producing the toxic gas.
The dioxide is the complete-combustion product; incompleteness gives the monoxide.
That gas tracks chlorine content, not oxygen supply.
Steam forms whenever hydrogen burns and is not the toxic concern.

check.stem: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous to people?

options.text: It reduces the capacity of the blood to carry oxygen
options.explanation: The gas binds where oxygen should travel, quietly starving the body of it.

options.text: It burns the skin on contact
options.explanation: Carbon monoxide is a gas breathed in; skin burning is not its harm.
It is toxic without any explosive behaviour.
Solvent action on plastics is irrelevant to its toxicity.

check.stem: Which benefit keeps incineration in use despite its hazards?

options.text: Polymers release a lot of heat energy when they burn
options.explanation: That heat can be recovered, which is why burning remains in the disposal mix.
Burning destroys the polymer; it never improves biodegradability.

options.text: Incineration produces no gases at all
options.explanation: The method is precisely the source of several hazardous gases.

options.text: Incineration needs no fuel to run
options.explanation: The polymer itself burns, but the claim of needing no fuel misses the point.

glossary.definition: Disposing of waste by burning it; polymers release heat energy but hazardous gases this way.
Chemically unreactive; addition polymers are inert because of their strong carbon-carbon bonds.
To be broken down naturally by micro-organisms; addition polymers are unable to do this.
A site where waste is buried in the ground, filling quickly with non-biodegrading polymers.
Poisonous to living things; hydrogen chloride and carbon monoxide are both toxic gases.
